locations.excerpt: Puzzle 3. The name Semantic Scholar promises search by meaning—so a natural-language question ought to be exactly the query it handles best. It is not. In August 2026, Is there an open access citation advantage returned just 13 results, for a topic with hundreds of relevant papers. Strip the question down to its keywords— open access citation advantage —and the same system returned about 35,300. Same information need, same words at its core, a 2,700-fold difference in results. Why did the more natural query retrieve dramatically less?

Figure 1.7 Observed behaviour in August 2026: the natural-language question returned 13 results, while the unquoted keyword query returned about 35,300. The contrast establishes a difference in visible behaviour; it does not reveal how Semantic Scholar parsed or executed either query.

Semantic Scholar remains unresolved: the August 2026 result counts tell us what happened, not where meaning entered the pipeline. We do not yet have the distinctions needed to ask whether retrieval itself was lexical, retrieval itself used dense representations, semantic processing occurred only after retrieval, or several stages were combined. The third puzzle therefore has to wait for Part II.

Puzzle 3 began with an expectation created by a name and an interface. Semantic Scholar sounds as though it searches by meaning, perhaps through dense retrieval over embeddings, so a natural-language question seems like the query the system should handle best. Yet in August 2026, Is there an open access citation advantage returned only 13 results—far fewer than the hundreds of relevant papers expected for this established topic—while the compact keyword query open access citation advantage returned about 35,300. Why did the supposedly more natural query retrieve dramatically less?

Puzzle 3 · Semantic Scholar Resolved as to architecture — from a document A natural-language question returned 13 results where the keywords returned about 35,300. The vendor’s published technical account describes lexical first-stage retrieval and a learnt reranker over a capped candidate set. That settles the dense-retrieval assumption; the exact cause of the August 2026 counts remains unproven. Without that account, this one would have joined the other two. Chapter 7’s account .

locations.excerpt: The lexical floor survives the learning. A purely lexical scoring model must match at least one term, and that has not changed. What changes is that the floor now applies to the expanded term set rather than the words as typed. That is how a sparse system running on an inverted index can retrieve a document sharing no typed word with the query—without becoming dense. As a concrete literature-review example, Elicit described work on SPLADE in June 2024: model-suggested related terms enrich the query before they are sent to regular full-text search . That account describes work under way when it was written rather than a settled production architecture.

The two variants are not equally visible in this sector, and the asymmetry itself tells you something. Learnt sparse retrieval has a named academic development example in Elicit; the cited account does not confirm production deployment. Late interaction does not appear to have a comparable publicly documented deployment in a major academic search product —it is well represented in the research literature and in general-purpose retrieval infrastructure, less so on a vendor’s architecture page. The storage cost described above is the usual explanation offered. Absence of documentation is not evidence of absence, and this is exactly the kind of claim that dates, so treat it as a description of what is currently inspectable rather than of what exists.

Representation boundary Not every apparent expansion is query transformation. SPLADE can assign weight to terms the searcher never typed, but what it produces is a weighted vocabulary representation, whereas an LLM rewrite produces text or a structured expression. Both outputs can be inspected, and either can be passed between components— Elicit’s described SPLADE approach feeds expanded terms to a full-text engine—so a component boundary is not what separates them. They are different forms of retrieval input. Product descriptions may call either query enrichment or expansion.

Elicit’s 13 June 2024 engineering post describes SPLADE work in progress, not a confirmed production rollout. Its changelog entry for 25 July 2024 subsequently announces unlimited search, summaries and chat and removal of credits. The timing is suggestive of lower search-serving costs, potentially from a SPLADE deployment, but that is an inference rather than confirmation: neither source attributes the pricing change to SPLADE or reports its deployment costs. Pricing can also reflect commercial decisions or other engineering changes. It does not establish that SPLADE is generally cheaper than BM25 or dense retrieval. Sources checked 12 September 2026.

locations.excerpt: Scopus AI routes. Rather than always running both paths, it can decide per question whether to search lexically, to search over vector embeddings, or to do both. Selecting a route and combining results are separate decisions: a run that takes one path combines nothing and is not hybrid under this book’s definition. A run that takes both still needs a fusion rule to merge what they return. The answer to “is this a lexical search or a vector search?” may therefore differ from one query to the next, and neither answer is wrong.

Scopus AI’s routing is the smallest useful illustration of adaptive control. The system decides, per question, whether to search lexically, over embeddings, or both. That is a single choice among three constrained routes, made before retrieval; it does not compose a multi-action trajectory. The lexical and vector paths are unchanged by being selected. The routing decision can still be right or wrong for a given question, and a librarian may want to see it recorded.

The lesson is not that Scopus AI is the best or worst design. It is that “RAG Fusion” is not a new kind of search: it is a particular composition of query transformation, dense retrieval and rank fusion, with generation appended. A reader of this book can therefore ask precise questions of it—how many variants, generated by what, retrieved against which index, fused at what depth, and how many merged results actually reach the context—where the label alone invites none. One caution against conflation: Chapter 10 used Scopus AI as its example of routing between lexical and vector paths. The mechanisms are compatible: routing chooses which paths run, while RAG Fusion combines lists from query variants. A product could do both, but these differently dated accounts do not establish exactly how later Scopus AI modes combine them.

locations.excerpt: Consider the query that returns nothing. In a conventional catalogue that is the end of the interaction: the searcher is told there are no results and left to work out why. I tested the alternative by pointing a model, through an MCP server , at my own library’s Primo index, and replaying database searches drawn from our 2023 zero-result logs under the template search for a database in Primo for X . The work is written up as “ What Changes When an LLM Agent Searches Your Library Catalogue? ” (June 2026). Two limits belong with it: the examples were selected rather than sampled, and 2026 models were answering 2023 queries. Read what follows as an exploratory demonstration of failure recovery, not a measured success rate.

A user looking for databases on autism gets nothing, because no database is called that. The loop broadens—psychology, medicine, education, disability—and returns PsycINFO, Education Research Complete and SocINDEX. cost of living becomes inflation, household expenditure and consumer prices, and reaches the economics databases. Rolex watches is recognised as a question about luxury goods and produces Statista and Passport. Misspellings resolve on the way past: statis to Statista, refinituv to LSEG—though that last one is where the dating problem bites hardest, since the rebrand it recovers postdates the query, and a 2026 model knows it in a way a 2023 one might not.

This is the strongest evidence in the book for a claim Chapters 3 and 4 made on other grounds: lexical retrieval is not obsolete. Wrapped in something that can fail and retry, an ordinary keyword search outperformed a cleverer single rewrite over the same index.

locations.excerpt: Scopus AI is documented more thinly. In Elsevier’s 2024 account, it expands a question into multiple query variants, fuses the retrieved lists using what Elsevier calls “RAG Fusion”, and generates a Topic Summary or Expanded Summary with references required for claims.

RRF has also travelled beyond hybrid retrieval. Elsevier’s 2024 account of Scopus AI’s “RAG Fusion” describes applying this formula—not to lexical and dense lists for one query, but to the ranked lists returned by several generated variants of the same question, before a summary is written from the merged top results. Nothing about RRF changes when it moves inside a generative product; the composition is worked through in Appendix G .

Elsevier has described the search module as follows: a user’s query is expanded by a language model into several variant queries; vector search runs against each variant; the resulting ranked lists are merged with reciprocal rank fusion; and the summary is generated from the top merged results, with references required for claims. The technique, called RAG Fusion , originated in Raudaschl’s prototype work and was released as open source before appearing in the product; Rackauckas (2024) provides a published description and evaluation, and Elsevier’s own account confirms the pipeline. As elsewhere in this book, the description is as documented in 2024; the product has since added further modes, and details should be re-verified rather than assumed.

The lesson is not that Scopus AI is the best or worst design. It is that “RAG Fusion” is not a new kind of search: it is a particular composition of query transformation, dense retrieval and rank fusion, with generation appended. A reader of this book can therefore ask precise questions of it—how many variants, generated by what, retrieved against which index, fused at what depth, and how many merged results actually reach the context—where the label alone invites none. One caution against conflation: Chapter 10 used Scopus AI as its example of routing between lexical and vector paths. The mechanisms are compatible: routing chooses which paths run, while RAG Fusion combines lists from query variants. A product could do both, but these differently dated accounts do not establish exactly how later Scopus AI modes combine them.
